terra.problem: Saul is under a tree at Migron, not identified as sitting at home. The text also does not say he has no idea where Jonathan is.
The text places Saul under the tree, but does not say the six hundred troops are standing under it.
The text does not say the troops are sitting with Saul under the tree.
The troops did not know Jonathan had left, but that does not establish that nobody saw him go.
The text does not say Jonathan slipped away or that nobody spotted him.
The text describes cliffs, but does not say there are no rivers or water in the area.
The explanation repeats the cliffs-versus-rivers contrast without much personality or a fresh observation.
The text describes cliffs but does not say there are no towers in the area.
The last sentence assigns Jonathan a reason and describes what he is looking at without marking it as a guess.
The explanation guesses what Jonathan would have done under a different belief and assumes he had been under the pomegranate tree.
Saying the call sounds like a threat to the Philistines assigns them a perception the text does not state.
The text says Jonathan climbed on his hands and feet, with his armor-bearer behind him. It does not say both men climbed on their hands and feet.
The text says the Philistines fell before Jonathan, but does not say nobody closed in on him.
The text credits the first assault to Jonathan and his armor-bearer together. It also does not state what two men could or could not have done on their own.
The commotion increases, but the text does not specifically say it gets louder.
The explanation gives the increasing commotion as Saul's reason for stopping, but the text does not state his reason or say he stopped talking.
The kitchen-timer comparison makes light of a scene in which people are attacking one another with swords.
The text says the Philistines are confused and wielding swords against their neighbors, not that they cannot tell who is who.
The text describes total confusion, but does not say nobody is lined up.
The text does not say the hills empty out or give a speed for their departure.
The Israelites join the pursuit, but the text does not say they leave the hills.
About six hundred troops were with Saul earlier. By the end of the passage, other Hebrews and Israelites have joined the battle, so that is not the stated size of the army at the end.
